newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Build takes edge off U.S. gasoline rally.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Build takes edge off U.S. gasoline rally.

text.p: A seasonal build in gasoline stocks took the edge off a rally that propelled unleaded gasoline futures to contract highs this week, analysts said on Tuesday.

The American Petroleum Institute estimated gasoline on hand at U.S. refineries rose 1.93 million barrels last week, dampening concerns that domestic supplies could tighten as a result of a refinery strike in France.
"It was a stretch to say that the Elf strike was fueling a rally in gasoline," said William Brown of W.H. Brown & Co Inc.
"What the data confirm is that underlying gasoline demand is ok, but it is not screaming," Brown said.

Based on the trade group's estimates, implied demand for gasoline eased to 7.2 million barrels per day (bpd) in the week leading up to the Thanksgiving Day holiday weekend, down from about 8 million bpd in the prior weeks.
Essentially, wholesalers had drawn enough gasoline stocks into secondary storage to meet the holiday demand, leaving inventories to build back up again at U.S. refineries.
"We were due for a correction," Brown said.

January unleaded gasoline surged to a contract-high 69.70 cents a gallon ahead of the API report, and bids were a penny off the high at 68.70 in ACCESS after-hours trade following release of the trade group's weekly refined products survey.

Spot gasoline prices eased in the Midwest ahead of the API estimates, which confirmed perceptions of increased stocks in the region. The trade group said gasoline supplies in primary storage at PADD II, Midwest refiners rose a net 1.7 million barrels, accounting for the bulk of the build in U.S. stocks.
On the crude oil side of the equation, API estimated crude inventories were drawn down 868,000 barrels last week and remained 17.86 million barrels below levels at the same week last year.

Analysts attributed the crude draw to a steep drop in crude imports in recent weeks. For the week ended November 29, U.S. refiners imported an average 6.48 million barrels of crude oil a day, down 1.05 million barrels from the same week last year.
"I don't think there's any problem with crude availability worldwide, I just think we are a less attractive market right now," Brown said.
The resumption of Iraqi oil exports, which some analysts say may be just weeks away, is expected to trim crude prices in Europe, reopening the arb to the United States, he said.
Distillate stocks remained 15.06 million barrels below the same week last year nationwide despite a net 1.85 million barrel build on the week, API said.
The week-on-week build masked a 1.15 million barrel draw in high sulphur diesel in the Northeast, where heating oil stocks remained 12.47 million barrels below the same week last year.
